analysis.one_liner: Bans selling, renting, or providing unsafe cribs, including at hotels and daycares.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support in January 2004, the Infant Crib Safety Act never received a committee hearing or vote and died in the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for businesses — manufacturers, sellers, thrift and consignment shops, rental companies, hotels, and daycares — to make, sell, resell, lease, or provide cribs that are unsafe for infants. A crib would be presumed unsafe unless it met existing federal safety regulations and industry safety standards, and the Consumer Product Safety Commission could enforce the rules with the same penalties it uses for other product safety violations. It targeted the secondhand crib market in particular, since most crib deaths happen in old, hand-me-down cribs.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with infants. The bill's own findings say more than 11,500 children age 2 and under are hurt in cribs badly enough each year to need hospital treatment, at least 26 children age 4 and under die from crib injuries each year, and most crib deaths occur in secondhand, hand-me-down, or heirloom cribs. Banning the commercial sale, resale, and rental of unsafe cribs — and requiring hotels to offer only safe cribs — would remove those hazards from the market and from the places families travel and leave their children.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any business to manufacture, sell, resell, lease, or otherwise place an unsafe crib into commerce — closing a gap in existing law, which the bill's findings say is inadequate to deal with dangerous secondhand cribs.
Requires hotels, motels, and similar lodging to provide only cribs that meet safety standards, protecting traveling families who rely on hotel cribs.
Applies to daycares, childcare facilities, and rental businesses that use or lease cribs, not just retailers — covering the places infants actually sleep away from home.
Gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission power to enforce the rules and apply the same penalties as other product safety violations, so the ban has teeth.

Targets the biggest documented hazard: the bill cites CPSC data that most crib deaths occur in secondhand, hand-me-down, or heirloom cribs, and that 11,500 children age 2 and under are injured in cribs each year.

analysis.who_pays: Crib manufacturers, retailers, thrift and consignment shops, furniture rental and leasing businesses, hotels and motels, and childcare providers, who would have to verify, replace, or stop dealing in cribs that do not meet federal and industry safety standards. The Consumer Product Safety Commission would bear the cost of enforcement, and the federal government would collect and pursue penalties. Ordinary families would keep their existing exemption — the bill explicitly does not apply to a one-time private sale of a used crib by an individual.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crib sellers, thrift stores, hotels, daycares

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall heavily on small operators — thrift stores, consignment shops, furniture rental firms, hotels, and home daycares — which would have to verify that every used crib they handle meets current federal regulations and ASTM standards or get rid of it.

Because the bill restricts commercial resale of used cribs, it could shrink the supply of cheap secondhand cribs, and low-income families who rely on the used market might face higher costs — though the bill preserves a family's right to sell or give away a crib in a one-time private sale.

A crib would be presumed unsafe unless it conformed not only to federal regulations but also to ASTM voluntary standards 'and any amendments' to them, meaning businesses would have to track industry standards that change over time, with civil penalties under the Consumer Product Safety Act for violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest and targeted at businesses, while the benefit is measured in infant lives — the bill's findings cite at least 26 deaths and more than 11,500 hospital-treated injuries a year, concentrated in old secondhand cribs that the bill would pull from commercial channels. The private-sale exemption protects ordinary families' garage sales and hand-me-downs, keeping the burden on professional sellers and operators. On balance, a well-designed child safety measure whose main downside is compliance work for small businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on January 22, 2004, joined by Senator Peter Fitzgerald, a Republican.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
Four senators — three Democrats and one Republican — signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill support from both parties.
No further action of any kind was taken: the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that sell, rent, or provide used cribs — thrift stores, resellers, hotels, and childcare operators — were spared new compliance duties and potential federal penalties, while families with infants got no new protection against unsafe cribs.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's support was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with Republican co-sponsorship and cosponsors from both parties — while the Republican-run Commerce Committee simply never moved it.

industries.industry: Secondhand crib sellers (thrift stores, consignment shops, resellers)
industries.note: The bill's core target: commercial sellers of used cribs could no longer resell, lease, or move unsafe used cribs into the market. Since most crib deaths happen in secondhand cribs, the industry's cost of weeding out or replacing old cribs buys the bill's main safety benefit.
Lodging facilities would be barred from offering unsafe cribs to guests and would face CPSC penalties for violations, forcing them to audit and replace crib inventories.

Explicitly covered as commercial users of cribs, daycares would have to ensure every crib meets current standards. Their interest in low costs pulls against the safety of the children they care for, though their core mission is aligned with it.

New-crib makers already must meet the federal standards the bill incorporates, and the ASTM standards are industry-developed, so the added burden is mainly certification and record-keeping. A safer market reputation also benefits compliant manufacturers.
